title: Making Introductions
goal: Give your name, connect your name to a useful detail, and introduce another person.

runs.text: identifies you. A full name, first name, job or connection can help the other person understand who you are. Choose the detail the encounter needs.

. The location does not prescribe one level of formality. If someone gives a preferred name or title, you can use that information rather than guessing their preference.

as a formal introductory greeting. It can be returned with the same greeting; it is not asking you to describe how you do your work. It is an optional expression here, not a required first-meeting formula.

runs.text: An introduction should give both people a way to continue. A shared activity is one possibility; an immediate personal question is not required.
If you have spoken online but are meeting physically for the first time, try
It's nice to finally meet in person
. Meeting and seeing formulas have flexible uses; do not turn them into a rigid test of whether contact happened before.
Could you say your name again?
asks for the letters. Chapter 4 develops repair; these two questions are available here when needed.
Use these fictional cards first. Then substitute real details if you want. On your own, speak both sides and change roles on the second attempt.

rows.text: A designer; on the design team; goes by Taylor
A researcher; on the research team; goes by Morgan
Taylor's friend; takes a photography class with Taylor

runs.text: You are Avery at a gathering. Introduce yourself to Morgan with your connection to Taylor. Supply Morgan's acknowledgment and your reply.
You are Taylor at a project meeting. Give your name and team. Morgan asks what to call you. Answer with your preferred name.
Introduce Morgan and Avery to each other. Avery asks how Morgan knows Taylor; Morgan says they work together.
We've met before, at the workshop
. Acknowledge that instead of pretending the introduction is new.
Hide the cards. Make a three-turn introduction using your own name or an invented identity. Ask for the name again if needed.
Hi, I'm Avery. I'm a friend of Taylor's. — I'm Morgan. Nice to meet you. — You too.
I'm Taylor Brooks. I'm on the design team. — What should I call you? — Please call me Taylor.
Morgan, this is Avery. Avery, this is my colleague Morgan. — Nice to meet you. How do you know Taylor? — We work together.
Oh, yes. Good to see you again.
Did the other person learn who you are and why you are connected? Did both people receive an introduction? Did you respond to what they actually said? Several wordings can succeed.

ja: 名前と、つながりを伝える。
note: 名前のあとに、ここにいる理由を一つ。仕事の場面では役割を添え、人を紹介するときは両方の人に声をかけます。
